This is a within-node tension, because easy verbal access to the trauma is hard to square with marked fragmentation and severe re-experiencing-linked formulation here.

vignette: James is a 57-year-old North American man who has been leading a solitary life since his traumatic experience. He works as a tutor, spending most of his days in libraries and small study rooms where he helps students with their homework and exam preparation. His trauma-a sexual assault-occurred several months ago and has left deep psychological scars that continue to affect his daily functioning. The attack happened one evening when James was walking home from work. He had stopped at a nearby park, intending only to rest on a bench for a moment before heading back to his apartment. It was there that he encountered the man who would assault him. The sudden and overwhelming physical force and loss of autonomy left an indelible mark on James. Since then, any form of physical touch or being in close proximity with men has become overwhelmingly triggering. James's daily routine is now a careful dance around his triggers and fears. He avoids situations that might evoke strong emotions, which he finds unsettling and overwhelming. His smoking habit has escalated as a coping mechanism, providing some semblance of comfort amidst the chaos of his thoughts. Any form of physical contact, even something as simple as a handshake or a pat on the back from a student, makes him feel exposed and vulnerable. In his role as a tutor, James finds himself increasingly isolated. He avoids being alone with male students for fear that it might trigger unwanted memories. This has led to some strained relationships at work; he has had to decline invitations to after-school events or collaborative study sessions where the presence of other men would be unavoidable. James's constant vigilance is palpable in his interactions and daily life. He watches others closely, constantly on the lookout for signs that they might harm him. This heightened state of alertness has made it difficult for James to trust anyone, leaving him feeling isolated and set apart from others. His choice of seating always reflects his need to feel safe; he positions himself in a corner where he can see everyone but remains out of reach. The vivid memory of the assault is ever-present in James's mind, with clear and detailed images that replay like a haunting movie. Yet, there are also gaps-times when memories feel incomplete, leaving him feeling fragmented and unsure about what truly happened. The inability to fully articulate his experience has left James feeling disconnected from others, as if he cannot adequately share or explain what haunts him. James's negative appraisals of himself and the world around him have become deeply ingrained. He no longer trusts his own body and feels that it betrayed him during the assault. His constant vigilance is a coping mechanism, but it has also led to an overwhelming sense of isolation and disconnection from others. What finally brought James to seek help was a particularly triggering incident at work. A male colleague had asked James to stay late to review some materials with a group of students, and James's fear and anxiety reached a breaking point. He realized that his life had become a series of avoidances, and he longed for the ability to reconnect with others without the constant fear of being harmed again. James is most afraid of never feeling safe again and living in perpetual isolation. However, he also hopes to find a way to reclaim some sense of normalcy and trust-both in himself and in those around him. His journey towards healing will involve navigating these fears while finding ways to rebuild his shattered sense of safety and trust.
